newsitem.title: USA: Dlr, US assets to benefit from EMU doubts -- experts.
newsitem.headline: Dlr, US assets to benefit from EMU doubts -- experts.

text.p: The dollar and U.S. financial assets will likely lure global investors as the defeat of the austerity-minded majority in France fuelled doubts about the European Monetary Union (EMU), experts said Sunday.

"We are looking at a weak Euro or no Euro at all," senior analyst Chris Turner at I.D.E.A., an advisory firm, said of the outlook for the single European currency following the opposition Socialist Party's victory in the French parliamentary elections.
The euro is scheduled for launch Jan. 1, 1999.
The Socialists won in a country plagued by unemployment on a pro-growth, pro-job platform and against the fiscal austerity required to meet the Maastricht criteria.

Their victory highlights two crucial issues for the Euro -- how strictly will the Maastricht Treaty's fiscal discipline criteria be interpreted and, thus, how many nations will be allowed to join the monetary union in 1999.

"The Socialists' victory seems to favour a weak Euro rather than no Euro at all. But, definitely, this is prime time for the speculators," Turner stressed. "People will be concerned and buy dollars, and, in general, the non-EMU currencies."
Turner expected speculators to pressure, in turn, the German mark if the "weak Euro" scenario prevailed or the other European currencies if the "no Euro" scenario emerges.

"If the single currency seems to be going ahead on time, the market will be betting on a broad and weak Euro," Turner said. "But as soon as Germany starts criticising France, that is when we'll go from a weak Euro to no Euro at all."

Goldman, Sachs International vice chairman Robert Hormats said the French elections showed "there is a limit to how much the citizens of the European democracies can tolerate in terms of higher taxes and cuts in social programmes."
Hormats added Europe's reluctance for more austerity is why the French Socialists "want the (Maastricht debt) criteria watered down and (German Chancellor Helmut) Kohl wants to revalue the gold."
He predicted Europe's new policy "will have a substantial effect on currency markets and U.S. asset markets."

"The U.S. markets are going to be a place of refuge," Hormats predicted. "American capital was starting to move to Europe on the view Europe would undertake a major restructuring. If that does not materialise, some of the money will be coming back here."
Hormats cautioned "the probability now is for an EMU based on watered-down criteria, with a broader and less rigorous adherence to the Maastricht criteria and a weaker Euro."
As a result, "the German bondholder who also is the German electorate may become upset and unwilling to support a Euro much weaker than the D-mark," he added.
"There will be a lot more room for speculators to test the central banks at this point," Hormats concluded.
John Lonski, senior economist at Moody's Investors Services, agreed the "outlook for the EMU is more uncertain," with "further dilution of the EMU criteria" to be expected.
